slides.title: Food odor organizes source-directed walking
body: **Chemoreception** is the detection of chemicals by sensory cells. Clawed lobsters, _Homarus americanus_, use dissolved food odors while walking across the seabed. Moore, Scholz and Atema compared paths toward mussel extract with paths recorded during otherwise equivalent raw-seawater delivery.

Odor-search paths contained pauses, sideways movement and backward steps while still progressing toward the source. Mean walking speed was 5.94 cm/s during odor trials, compared with 10.81 cm/s in controls. Faster movement therefore did not necessarily indicate better source-directed searching.

The trajectories demonstrate that chemical stimulation reorganizes locomotion under flowing-water conditions. Only motivated, successful approaches were included in the detailed analysis, so these measurements do not estimate the success probability of all lobsters. They also do not identify the neurons that select each correction.

slides.title: A flume separates chemical input from water flow
body: A **flume** is a channel that supplies controlled flowing water. Moore and colleagues tested lobsters in a 250 × 90 × 20 cm arena with a current of 1.0 cm/s. A reference grid and overhead video allowed position and heading to be measured.

Mussel extract at 0.5 g/L was delivered at 50 mL/min from a source 9 cm above the bottom. Control trials substituted raw seawater while retaining delivery conditions. Rostrum positions were digitized once per second, providing a common spatial and temporal reference for comparisons.

These controls attribute behavioral differences to the presence of the food extract rather than the existence of current or a delivery tube alone. The extract is a mixture, not an identified receptor ligand. Its source concentration also differs from the fluctuating concentration reaching the animal downstream.

slides.title: Speed and heading change during the approach
body: **Heading angle** describes the direction of the lobster’s body relative to upstream. Moore and colleagues grouped recorded behavior by distance from the source. This analysis asks whether the approach is uniform or changes as chemical and mechanical conditions change.

From 240 to 110 cm away, mean speed increased from 2.3 to 7.8 cm/s while heading decreased from 98.8° to about 20°. Between 110 and 40 cm, speed remained near 7 cm/s. Within the final 40 cm, speed fell toward 4.7 cm/s and heading increased toward 37°.

These transitions establish distinct movement regimes during successful searching. They are consistent with changing sensory guidance near the source, but distance covaries with plume structure and concentration. The experiment therefore does not establish a dedicated neuronal distance code or prove that one chemical gradient causes every transition.

slides.title: Recorded turns do not reveal a fixed casting program
body: **Turning angle** is the change in movement direction between successive path segments. Moore and colleagues compared heading and turn distributions in odor-search trials. A stereotyped alternating search program would predict consistently organized counterturns rather than the observed broad variation among paths.

Experimental headings were centered around 0–10°, and turns around 10–20°. Individual animals followed variable paths across repeated trials. Odor stimulation supported an upstream bias without producing a single characteristic path that every lobster repeated at fixed intervals.

The findings weaken a simple invariant counterturn account for this preparation. They do not exclude central motor programs altogether: sensory feedback could modify an internally generated movement sequence. The data also leave open how bilateral antennular input and water-flow information contribute to the observed directional corrections.

slides.title: Close-range searching recruits walking-leg raking
body: Moore and colleagues measured **leg raking**, repeated movements that bring walking-leg sensory surfaces into contact with the local environment. They compared raking rates at several distances from the odor source, testing whether close-range searching involves more than antennular sampling.
Raking averaged 3.4 events per 5 s within 7 cm of the source, 2.6 at 7–15 cm, and 1.15 at 15–22 cm. Beyond 22 cm it averaged only 0.1 per 5 s. Most recorded raking therefore occurred near the source.

The change supports recruitment of near-substrate sampling during final localization. A switch from antennular guidance to leg-based guidance was the authors’ interpretation, rather than a selective-lesion result in this study. Increased raking could also accompany contact exploration or feeding preparation, so its sensory cause requires separate tests.

slides.title: Two antennular pathways can guide spiny lobsters
body: The Caribbean spiny lobster, _Panulirus argus_, differs from the clawed lobster used in the earlier flume study. Its antennules carry **aesthetascs**, specialized olfactory hairs, together with non-aesthetasc sensilla containing other chemical and mechanical sensory neurons. These populations offer potentially overlapping information.

Horner, Weissburg and Derby tested 48–74 mm carapace-length animals in a 5,000-L flume with flow near 5 cm/s. Shrimp extract at 3 or 0.3 g/L supplied high- and low-odor treatments; seawater supplied a chemical control. Selective manipulations targeted different sensory populations on both antennules.

The experiment asks whether one pathway is indispensable for food-source localization under realistic flow. A preserved response after removing one population can show that the remaining pathway is sufficient in this assay. It cannot establish that the populations are identical or redundant in every natural behavior.

slides.title: Selective lesions require distinct procedural controls
body: Horner and colleagues used several interventions because sensory hairs can contain different neuron types. Shaving removed about 99.8% of aesthetascs. Removing and sealing non-aesthetasc sensilla targeted another pathway, while a 15-min distilled-water treatment temporarily impaired antennular chemosensitivity.

The source was positioned 2 m upstream of release. High and low shrimp concentrations were compared with seawater, and animals were offered shrimp afterward to check feeding motivation. Some manipulations also affected mechanoreceptors, an important qualification when interpreting a failure to orient.

The combination separates chemical guidance from complete loss of appetite more effectively than a lesion alone. Distilled-water treatment is reversible over approximately 24 h, but is not a molecularly selective receptor knockout. The conclusions concern the sensory populations affected by each treatment and the particular flow assay.

slides.title: Either pathway can preserve food-source finding
body: Horner and colleagues measured the proportion of lobsters reaching the odor source after selective bilateral sensory manipulation. Intact animals found the high-odor source in 68% of trials and the low-odor source in 45%; no intact animal located a seawater source.

After aesthetasc removal, success remained 77% for high odor and 69% for low odor. Removing non-aesthetasc chemo-mechanosensory sensilla also preserved source finding, at 64% and 45%. In contrast, eliminating antennular chemoreceptor input broadly produced very poor localization.

Either retained antennular chemical pathway can therefore support this food-search task. The results do not show that aesthetascs are unnecessary for all olfactory functions or that increased percentages demonstrate an improvement caused by removal. Variable success and the different effects of each manipulation must be interpreted within the tested preparation.

slides.title: Successful searching can still become less efficient
body: **Net-to-gross displacement ratio**, or NGDR, is straight-line displacement divided by total path length. A value closer to one indicates a straighter route. Horner and colleagues measured this variable separately from eventual source-finding success, together with arrival time, speed and heading.

At high odor concentration, mean NGDR was 0.82 in controls, compared with 0.63 after aesthetasc removal and 0.62 after non-aesthetasc chemo-mechanosensory removal. Mean arrival times across treatment groups were at most 96 s for high odor and 176 s for low odor.

Remaining sensory pathways can preserve arrival while losing efficient progress. Those times are group means, not upper limits for every animal. The altered routes show a contribution to search performance but do not identify whether the missing information concerned concentration, timing, flow direction or the reliability of bilateral comparisons.

slides.title: Turbulence produces patchy dissolved odor input
body: An **odor plume** is the distribution of odor-bearing water transported downstream from a source. Reidenbach and Koehl visualized plumes using **planar laser-induced fluorescence**, or PLIF: a thin laser sheet excites dissolved dye, and calibrated camera intensity estimates local concentration.

Their 25-m flume produced fine odor filaments separated by cleaner water. Images were recorded at 60 frames/s, yielding 16.7-ms temporal resolution. Measurements at different lateral positions showed a denser central plume and sparser encounters toward its edge.

The images establish the physical input available to a sensory appendage, rather than recording receptor activation. Fluorescent dye is a transport tracer and need not bind lobster odor receptors. A smooth time-averaged concentration field therefore conceals the intermittent encounters and gaps that a moving animal actually samples.

slides.title: Antennular length changes the sampled chemical pattern
body: Reidenbach and Koehl placed virtual sampling lines within measured PLIF images to represent the aesthetasc-bearing portion of an antennule. Lobster and blue-crab geometries were compared at the same 8-cm height. This approach separates appendage geometry from differences in chemical receptor sensitivity.

The lobster sampler flicked at 2 Hz and moved at 6 cm/s during the downstroke. The crab sampler was only 2 mm long and flicked at 3 Hz. Lobster geometry intercepted odor during more flicks and sampled higher peak concentrations than crab geometry.

Longer sampling structures can encounter more filaments, while faster sampling can partly compensate for shorter length. These are measurements extracted from real plume images using specified sampling assumptions. They do not show that an intact lobster consciously compares every point along its antennule or implements the authors’ analysis algorithm.

slides.title: Discrete sniffing changes the gaps between encounters
body: An **odor-free gap** is an interval without an encounter above the chosen detection threshold. Reidenbach and Koehl compared continuous concentration measurements with concentrations encountered by virtual flicking antennules. The comparison tests whether intermittent movement changes the timing of available chemical information.

Almost all gaps in continuously measured concentration were shorter than 500 ms throughout the sampled plume. Flicking antennules instead experienced longer gaps, and their gaps increased as downstream distance to the source decreased. Sampling schedule altered the input statistics before neural processing occurred.

The counterintuitive distance relationship shows why encounter frequency cannot be treated as a universal distance ruler. The result depends on plume transport, threshold and flicking geometry. It identifies available temporal cues but does not establish that a lobster uses this particular gap statistic to choose a turn.

body: Near the seabed, transport and mixing differ from conditions several centimeters above it. slides.title: Aesthetasc arrays organize the olfactory interface
body: **Aesthetascs** are thin-walled sensory hairs bearing the outer dendrites of olfactory receptor neurons. On a Panulirus lateral antennular flagellum, they occur in repeated rows bordered by larger guard hairs. The scanning electron micrographs reveal a structured array rather than a uniformly exposed sensory surface.

Reidenbach, George and Koehl measured biological geometry before constructing physical models. Representative aesthetasc diameter was 22 µm, length about 720 µm, and spacing about 60 µm. The hairs are arranged at an offset angle, allowing appendage orientation to influence the water entering their gaps.

Chemical detection requires molecules to reach this sensory interface before membrane receptors can respond. Microscopy establishes dimensions and arrangement, not channel opening or neural firing. Guard-hair function must therefore be tested through flow measurements rather than inferred solely from the presence of a protective-looking structure.

slides.title: Scaled physical models isolate hair-array hydrodynamics
body: A **dynamically scaled model** reproduces the important balance of fluid forces despite using enlarged structures and a different fluid. Reidenbach and colleagues built glass-rod hair arrays in mineral oil and matched the **Reynolds number**, the ratio of inertial to viscous effects relevant to flow.

Biological dimensions and flicking motions constrained the model geometry. **Particle-image velocimetry**, or PIV, tracked suspended particles between images to measure fluid velocity around and between hairs. The investigators varied orientation, speed and guard-hair presence while retaining the remaining preparation.

These controlled changes identify mechanical causes of water exchange that are difficult to measure inside a living hair array. The model contains no sensory neurons and measures no ligand binding. Its results establish physical delivery conditions that can influence olfaction, rather than a complete explanation of receptor transduction or behavior.

slides.title: The fast downstroke replaces water between hairs
body: An antennular flick consists of a fast downward movement followed by a slower return. In the scaled-model study, PIV measured water velocity inside the hair array during the downstroke. The published color map reports velocity rather than chemical concentration or sensory-neuron activity.

During the fast movement, water penetrated the aesthetasc gaps and replaced the previously retained sample. Measured profiles were comparatively uniform across the array. Separate high-speed recordings placed downstroke motion near an aesthetasc Reynolds number of 2, compared with about 0.5 during return.

The sensory organ therefore controls exposure mechanically before a receptor opens. Fresh water entering the gaps can deliver new odor molecules, but a flow map alone cannot establish which molecules bind or how many spikes are emitted. Reynolds-number estimates describe the biological movement studied, not a universal threshold for all crustacean hairs.

slides.title: The slow return retains a chemical sample
body: **Leakiness** describes the extent to which water passes through a hair array rather than around it. Reidenbach and colleagues compared measured downstroke and return-stroke flow. The slower return reduced penetration, allowing the captured water to remain near the aesthetasc surfaces.

Return motion was approximately one-quarter of downstroke speed, yet water between hairs moved about 25 times more slowly. The nonlinear change shows that reducing appendage speed can alter array permeability much more than it alters the movement of the appendage itself.

Retention creates time for molecular diffusion toward the sensory surface. The authors estimated that diffusion over 0.5 s could span about 32 µm; this is a physical calculation, not measured ligand uptake by neurons. The experiment establishes a sampling mechanism without proving which concentration history an individual receptor experiences.

slides.title: Hair orientation and guard hairs alter delivery
body: The shape and orientation of an aesthetasc array determine how incident water moves through it. Reidenbach and colleagues compared the observed zigzag orientation, offset by about 32°, with a zero-degree arrangement. They also measured arrays with and without surrounding guard hairs.

The observed orientation produced relatively uniform water penetration during the flick. Guard-hair removal changed the spatial velocity profile, revealing a hydrodynamic contribution beyond a possible protective role. The controlled physical model isolated these geometry effects without altering neuronal excitability.

The findings link anatomical arrangement to the distribution of a fresh sensory sample. They do not show that guard hairs detect food or that a particular flow profile automatically improves behavioral success. Sensory performance depends on subsequent diffusion, receptor activation and central interpretation, none of which was measured in the model.

slides.title: Published video directly reveals lobster sniffing
body: Koehl and colleagues programmed a mechanical lobster to flick real Panulirus antennules in a fluorescent dye plume. This preparation retained the biological hair array while controlling movement. Dye released from a benthic source 1 m upstream represented chemicals carried from a food source.

The original high-speed frames show approximately 1-mm-thick dye parcels entering the array during the rapid downstroke. During the slower return, dye remained trapped between hairs while the surrounding plume continued moving. A later downstroke shed that sample and captured another.

The observation directly supports discrete water sampling rather than uninterrupted exposure to ambient concentration. Fluorescent dye visualizes transported water and solute; it does not record food-odor receptor binding. The mechanically moved preparation also omits feedback by which an intact animal adjusts where and when to flick.

slides.title: A captured sample preserves spatial information briefly
body: Koehl and colleagues measured concentration along the aesthetasc-bearing section of the antennule through successive video frames. Their published **spatiotemporal map** places position on one axis and time on the other, with color representing measured dye concentration at each position.

The pattern changed during rapid downstrokes but remained comparatively stable during slower return and stationary intervals. Dye could spread along the antennule during acquisition, so the captured pattern was not an exact unchanged slice of the original plume. Sampling both retains and filters information.

This physical filtering precedes neuronal transduction. A spatially nonuniform retained sample could stimulate different sensory endings differently, but the paper did not record those cells or prove that the brain reconstructs the original spatial pattern. Mechanical retention therefore constrains the input without establishing a particular downstream code.

slides.title: Ionotropic-receptor genes occur in olfactory neurons
body: **Ionotropic receptors**, or IRs, are chemosensory proteins related to ionotropic glutamate receptors, a family of ligand-gated membrane channels. Corey and colleagues identified candidate IR sequences in Panulirus olfactory tissue and used in situ hybridization to locate their RNA within sensory cells.

IR25a and IR93a signals occurred broadly in olfactory receptor neurons. Antisense probes detect complementary target RNA; sense probes supplied negative controls for nonspecific staining. IR8a and another candidate showed more restricted expression, suggesting common components alongside more variable receptor populations.

The findings support an IR-based molecular architecture in lobster olfaction. Sequence similarity and cellular expression do not establish the ligand of a candidate receptor, its ion selectivity or the exact subunit composition of a native channel. Those properties require functional tests beyond staining for receptor RNA.

slides.title: Receptor protein reaches the sensory dendrites
body: RNA expression alone does not show where the resulting protein acts. Corey and colleagues used an antibody against IR25a to test its localization. Cross-sections through distal aesthetasc hairs supplied anatomical access to the outer dendrites, where transported odorants first approach olfactory neurons.

IR25a immunofluorescence occurred within the dendritic profiles. Sections stained without the primary antibody supplied a background control, and an antibody recognizing an Ih-channel protein provided a separate neuronal comparison. Western blots also detected a band near the predicted IR25a molecular mass of approximately 100 kDa.

The convergence of biochemical detection and dendritic staining places a candidate receptor component at a plausible transduction site. It does not demonstrate that every stained molecule forms an active surface channel. Antibody specificity, membrane localization and direct odor-evoked current are distinct evidentiary questions.

slides.title: Neighboring sensory cells differ in chemical selectivity
body: Corey and colleagues loaded sensory-cell clusters with a calcium-sensitive dye and applied different chemical stimuli. **Calcium imaging** reports changes in intracellular calcium through changing fluorescence. It can reveal many cells simultaneously, complementing measurements made from one neuron at a time.

The stimulus set included food extract, arginine and glutamate at 1 mM for the amino-acid tests. Neighboring cells showed different response profiles across the panel. A published heat map summarizes this heterogeneity rather than assigning one shared response to the whole cluster.

The responses establish chemical selectivity at the cellular level despite broad expression of common IR components. They do not identify which variable IR recognizes each ligand or prove that fluorescence amplitude equals membrane current. The association between expression and physiology motivates receptor tests but is not itself receptor deorphanization.

slides.title: Single-cell sequencing resolves receptor coexpression
body: Whole-organ sequencing combines RNA from sensory neurons, support cells and other tissue. Kozma and colleagues instead collected individual fluorescently identified olfactory sensory neurons for **single-cell transcriptomics**, sequencing the expressed RNA of each cell. This separates within-cell coexpression from differences between cell populations.

All seven analyzed single-cell transcriptomes contained IR25a and IR93a. They also contained variable tuning-IR transcripts, while IR8a and IR76b were not detected in those cells. The photographed collection pipette documents the cellular preparation used for sampling.

The result supports shared receptor components with cell-specific combinations of additional candidates. Seven cells cannot exhaust the entire sensory population, and a failure to detect an RNA need not mean the gene is absent from every neuron. Transcript detection also does not establish protein abundance or channel assembly.

slides.title: A neuron can express many candidate tuning receptors
body: **Tuning IRs** are variable receptor candidates proposed to contribute ligand selectivity alongside more widely expressed components. Kozma and colleagues compared their abundance across single olfactory sensory neurons. The original heat map displays receptor identity by row and cellular sample by column.

Each analyzed neuron contained 9–53 tuning-IR transcripts, often with only one or a few expressed at high abundance. This arrangement differs from a simple rule in which every sensory neuron expresses exactly one ligand-selective receptor. Shared coreceptors do not eliminate molecular diversity between cells.

The data constrain candidate combinations but do not show that all detected IRs enter the same membrane complex. Low-abundance transcripts could have different functions or reflect technical sampling. Receptor composition, surface delivery and ligand specificity require additional protein-localization and functional experiments.

slides.title: Gene expression does not establish odor recognition
body: Kozma and colleagues also examined **G-protein-coupled receptors**, or GPCRs, and **transient receptor potential** channels, or TRP channels, in sensory neurons. GPCRs can regulate intracellular signaling, whereas TRP proteins form ion channels with diverse sensory and cellular functions.

Individual cells expressed 12–17 GPCR candidates and overlapping sets of TRP-channel genes. The published summary includes common proteins and additional variable candidates. These transcript inventories reveal potential molecular machinery alongside the IR family rather than one fully resolved odor-transduction pathway.

Expression of a GPCR in an olfactory neuron does not prove that it binds a food odor; it may receive modulatory input. Likewise, a TRP transcript does not establish the channel carrying the primary receptor current. Connecting genes to mechanism requires ligand responses, channel properties and perturbations in identified cells.

slides.title: Controlled odor delivery separates input from response
body: Bobkov and colleagues recorded Panulirus sensory neurons in a semi-intact antennular preparation. Odor reached the outer dendrites while the cell bodies remained accessible to electrodes and imaging. Separate fluid compartments limited direct stimulation of somata and allowed repeated inputs to the sensory surface.

A fluorescent tracer characterized stimulus timing, while calcium imaging and loose-patch recordings measured responses. Food extract was tested at concentrations up to 0.5 mg/mL. Increasing pulse duration increased the effective delivered stimulus, but did not create a perfectly independent change in concentration alone.

These calibrations establish when chemical input arrived relative to cellular activity. They also expose an important experimental limitation: pulse duration, onset kinetics and effective dose can covary. Apparent concentration dependence must therefore be interpreted using the actual delivery waveform, rather than only the solution concentration stated at the source.

slides.title: Peripheral neurons can be excited or inhibited by odor
body: Bobkov and colleagues found tonic excitation, phasic–tonic excitation and inhibition among olfactory receptor neurons exposed to food extract. **Tonic** responses persist during stimulation; **phasic** responses emphasize its beginning. Inhibitory responses reduce activity relative to the cell’s unstimulated state.

Whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings near −70 to −60 mV measured inward or outward odor-evoked currents alongside firing patterns. Excitatory current could persist or adapt rapidly, while some cells showed inhibitory currents. Thus, diversity was already present in the receptor input, before central synaptic processing.

The observations reject an account in which all peripheral cells transmit the same excitation and the brain creates every inhibitory response. They do not resolve the molecular channel responsible for every current class. A current’s direction depends on holding voltage and ionic driving force, not simply the behavioral meaning of an odor.

slides.title: Calcium signals and spikes have different time courses
body: Calcium-sensitive fluorescence is often used as a proxy for neuronal activity, but it is not an action potential. Bobkov and colleagues recorded spikes and calcium simultaneously in identified lobster sensory neurons. The comparison tested how reliably a slower optical signal represents rapid electrical output.

Tonic, phasic–tonic and inhibitory neurons showed corresponding but differently filtered fluorescence changes. Calcium generally changed more slowly than the spike pattern. An inhibitory optical response could accompany reduced firing, while excitation increased firing and then accumulated a calcium signal.

The relationship supports calcium imaging for identifying response classes while limiting interpretations of precise encounter timing. Dye kinetics, intracellular buffering and calcium removal all intervene between spikes and fluorescence. A broad calcium peak cannot be assigned the same duration as the odor pulse or the underlying burst of spikes.

body: A **burst** is a cluster of spikes separated from another cluster by a quieter interval. body: Bobkov and colleagues imaged many sensory somata within the same antennular cluster and compared their calcium time series. **Correlation** measures the degree to which two signals vary together. slides.title: Cyclic nucleotides can support peripheral inhibition
body: A **second messenger** is an intracellular molecule whose concentration changes after signaling begins. Michel and Ache tested cyclic nucleotides in lobster sensory neurons that were excited by food extract but inhibited by proline. Whole-cell recordings were made at a holding voltage of −60 mV.

slides.title: Odor rapidly changes dendritic second messengers
body: Boekhoff and colleagues isolated membranes enriched from the outer dendrites of Panulirus olfactory hairs. A **quench-flow assay** mixes membrane material with stimulus and rapidly stops the reaction, allowing biochemical changes over milliseconds to be measured independently of spike output.

Food extract produced transient increases in cAMP and **inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate**, or IP3, peaking within approximately 50 ms. The assay establishes rapid odor-associated biochemical signaling in pooled dendritic material. It does not demonstrate that both messengers rise in every individual neuron, or that a measured rise directly opens a particular channel. Pooling, biochemical enrichment and separation from the intact organ limit cell-specific circuit interpretations.

body: Boekhoff and colleagues compared taurine and proline because individual ligands can excite one lobster sensory neuron yet inhibit another. slides.title: Odor-response probability depends on bursting phase
body: **Phase** describes where a neuron lies within its recurring burst cycle. Park and colleagues delivered comparable odor pulses at different times after the previous spontaneous burst. A population with different periods could jointly report encounter timing, but behavioral use of that information remains a further hypothesis.

slides.title: Plume intermittency supplies a different spatial statistic
body: **Intermittency** describes the temporal discontinuity of odor. Michaelis and colleagues quantified it as the count of concentration spikes crossing a threshold within a time window. Michaelis and colleagues used a turbulent-plume model validated against laboratory fluorescence and velocity measurements. They compared intermittency with concentration as potential information for aquatic odor-source tracking.

The model covered a 5 × 0.5 × 0.15 m domain with mean flow near 0.02 m/s. Intermittency profiles depended on cross-stream position and the observation window. At plume edges, bilateral differences in encounter frequency could remain informative when instantaneous concentration was unreliable.

These results propose a statistic that complements a mean concentration reading. The published profiles are model-derived and threshold dependent, not direct measurements of lobster navigation commands. Physical validation strengthens the plume representation but does not validate every assumption about sensory thresholds, memory windows or bilateral neural comparisons.

slides.title: Search combines sampling, neural timing and context
body: Michaelis and colleagues compared modeled intermittency estimates at different sampling frequencies and tested simulated search rules. The original figure shows how a finite observation window and sample schedule affect the estimated chemical statistic. This makes sampling strategy part of the navigation hypothesis rather than a passive detail.

Their results support temporal encounter information alongside concentration under specified plume conditions. Earlier measurements show why those conditions matter: flicking changes encounter gaps, bursting neurons respond according to recent history, and removing one antennular pathway can preserve arrival while reducing path straightness.

Together, the studies connect physical acquisition, peripheral coding and source-directed behavior without establishing every intervening synapse. A complete account must distinguish measured fluid patterns, recorded neuronal responses and actual animal trajectories. Neither a successful model search nor receptor expression alone proves the mechanism that a lobster uses in nature.

items.lead: Expression does not establish receptor function
items.text: IR localization and single-cell coexpression identify candidate machinery, but ligand specificity, channel composition and causal function require further tests.
Excitation, inhibition and intrinsic bursting occur in sensory neurons; phase-dependent responses can carry encounter-history information.
Central inhibition changes transmission, while plume and decoding models propose usable cues; their behavioral necessity remains to be demonstrated.
